query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the Mo fraction in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo by partially substituting Mo (e.g., with Zr) will lower the electronegativity difference and local lattice distortions, thereby enhancing room‐temperature plasticity while largely retaining the high yield strength associated with the disordered BCC solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo exhibiting a disordered BCC solid solution with a compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa and limited room‐temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Decrease the Mo content by partially substituting Mo with an equivalent molar amount of Zr (or a similar element from the NbZrTi-based family) while maintaining the overall alloy system.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature compression tests on as-cast or homogenized samples that preserve the single-phase disordered BCC structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the disordered BCC phase with reduced atomic-scale lattice distortions and a narrower electronegativity difference distribution.
generation.mechanism: The partial replacement of Mo reduces the mismatch in electronegativity and associated lattice strain, which in turn facilitates easier dislocation motion. This promotes enhanced plastic deformation without significantly compromising the solid solution strengthening responsible for high yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An observable increase in room-temperature plastic strain (improved ductility) with a yield strength that remains close to 1719 MPa, or experiences only a minor reduction, within the limits of maintaining a single-phase BCC structure.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy with limited plasticity and a compressive yield strength of ~1719 MPa.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected only if the modification maintains the disordered BCC phase. Excessive reduction of Mo or substitution with elements that are too dissimilar (in terms of atomic size or bonding characteristics) may lead to phase separation or intermetallic formation, negating the beneficial effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in ductility and the exact balance between strength and plasticity remain uncertain and require empirical calibration to determine the optimum substitution ratio.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of NbZrTiHfMo alloys with systematically reduced Mo content by partially substituting Mo with Zr. Maintain identical processing routes to ensure a disordered BCC phase. Conduct room-temperature compression tests and perform microstructural analysis (using XRD and SEM) to verify phase constitution.
measurements: Grain size and lattice parameter measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with reduced Mo content do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in plastic strain (with a corresponding maintenance of yield strength within an acceptable range, e.g., less than 15% reduction from 1719 MPa) or if undesired phases/intermetallic compounds are detected, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, Hf proved to be the optimal choice because it involved an increase in both σycal and Tmix, since it possessed the lowest shear modulus and highest atomic radius among the Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, and W elements and the highest melting point among the Cr, Hf, Ti, V, and Zr elements. Figure 6 shows the way in which the molar ratio of Hf affected the theoretical strength (v and melting temperature (Tmix) of MoNbTaW alloy systems. Although Tmix decreased with the addition of Hf, Tmix of equiatomic HfMoNbTaW was still higher than that of MoNbTaVW. Furthermore, the theoretical strength (σycal) increased 30.8% from 2393 to 3131 MPa during equiatomic addition of Hf into MoNbTaW and was thus significantly higher than that of MoNbTaVW. From the literature, we predict that the σycal may be higher than the real strength of an alloy, because the Gmix is referred to in our calculations, rather than the real shear modulus. The real shear modulus of MoNbTaVW is 75 GPa [], which is lower than the Gmix of 87.94 GPa.
